props.title: The Birth of a Nation
props.initialSlug: Epic Civil War drama that sparked fierce controversy

sections.content: The Birth of a Nation revolutionized filmmaking while simultaneously promoting deeply racist ideology. D.W. Griffith's technical innovations - parallel editing, close-ups, night photography, and elaborate battle sequences - created the grammar of modern cinema. The 3-hour epic was the first true American blockbuster, seen by millions and charging unprecedented ticket prices of $2 (equivalent to about $50 today). Yet its glorification of the Ku Klux Klan and use of white actors in blackface sparked protests by the NAACP and remains one of cinema's most controversial legacy pieces alongside Triumph of the Will (1935).

sections.content: The film's impact extended far beyond its era. Its racist depictions influenced American cinema's portrayal of Black characters for decades, establishing harmful stereotypes that directors like Oscar Micheaux actively fought against with films like Body and Soul (1925). Modern filmmakers continue grappling with its legacy - BlacKkKlansman (2018) directly incorporates footage to critique its racism, while Gone with the Wind (1939) echoed its romanticized view of the antebellum South.

Technically, the film's innovations appear in countless later works. Saving Private Ryan (1998) uses Griffith's battlefield tracking shots. The Lord of the Rings trilogy (2001-2003) employs his epic scope and parallel action cutting. Even Moonlight (2016) utilizes the intimate close-ups Griffith helped pioneer, though to radically different thematic effect. SUBHEAD: Technical Legacy vs. Cultural Damage

movies.title: Do the Right Thing
movies.slug: Spike Lee's masterpiece examining racial tensions, offering a modern counterpoint to Birth of a Nation's perspective

sections.content: Film scholars continue debating how to teach The Birth of a Nation, weighing its technical achievements against its propaganda. Daughters of the Dust (1991) director Julie Dash and 12 Years a Slave (2013) director Steve McQueen have discussed how the film's techniques can be reclaimed while rejecting its ideology. The controversy mirrors broader cultural discussions about separating artistic innovation from problematic content, seen in reactions to Gone with the Wind (1939) and The Jazz Singer (1927).
